chunks: Standard termination and Z0 values. The question: What are some standard termination/characteristic impedances?
Every cable and circuit-board trace has a characteristic impedance, the resistance it "looks like" to a fast signal.
A few values are industry standards: 50 ohms for radio gear, test equipment and most single traces, and 75 ohms for video.
Pairs of wires use 90, 100 or 120 ohms depending on the interface. The numbers are agreements.
Everything in the signal path must share the same number, or parts of the signal bounce back.
Think of railway gauge, the spacing between the two rails. Every track, train and station on a route has to use the same gauge.
If two sections differ, the train can't cross smoothly. Impedance works the same way: cable, connector, board trace and chip input all have to agree. The analogy has one gap.
A small mismatch doesn't stop the signal. It just sends back a small echo.
Loss (red) bottoms out near 77 ohms; power capacity (green) peaks near 30 ohms. At 50 ohms you pay about 10% more loss than the minimum and keep 86% of peak power.
That's the compromise. At 75 ohms loss is at its minimum but power capacity has dropped to about 56%.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance a wire "looks like" to a signal traveling along it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Single-ended: one signal wire measured against a ground or return path. Differential pair: two wires carrying opposite versions of one signal.
Its impedance is measured between the two wires.
Termination: a resistor at the end of a line, chosen to equal Z 0 so the signal is absorbed ("Impedance matching: what, why, when").
Reflection: the part of a signal that bounces back at a mismatch ("Reflections and why they matter").
Plug a 75 ohms video cable into a 50 ohms input on an oscilloscope (a measuring instrument). The size of the bounce is (50-75) over (50 plus 75) equals -0. 2 .
So a 1 volts step sends 0. 2 volts back, inverted. If both ends were 50 ohms, nothing would bounce.
The same idea holds for pairs: a USB pair is 90 ohms, and routing it at 100 ohms leaves a small mismatch. That is the whole idea.
"50 ohms is the default for RF, test gear and single-ended PCB traces, picked as a compromise between lowest loss near 77 ohms and highest power handling near 30 ohms in coax.
75 ohms is video, close to lowest loss. Differentials are mostly 100 ohms (Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS), 90 ohms for USB, about 85 ohms for PCIe, and 120 ohms for CAN and RS-485.
Terminations equal those values, so a 50 ohms line gets a 50 ohms load, and everything in the path has to share the number or you get reflections."
